title: Good Is the Enemy of Great
hook: The scanner glows green while the wait list everyone calls acceptable keeps one patient out of reach.
counterintuition: The paradox is that failure usually forces a conversation while competent numbers can avoid one. The mistaken move is treating a good benchmark as permission to stop looking; the better move is to compare it with harder evidence until comfort has to answer.
tryThisNow: Put one result you call good beside one ignored consequence from the same work, then write the sharper comparison that would make the gap impossible to wave away.
keyTakeaway: Good becomes dangerous when it protects a weaker standard from scrutiny and lets people mistake acceptable performance for sustained, compounding strength.

breakdown.fastRead:
The MRI console glows green, the monthly report is clean, and the delayed follow-up list sits under a binder clip. That is the danger: good performance can look like closure while the harder evidence keeps waiting.

Good is the enemy of great when acceptable results become a shield. A benchmark can prove competence and still hide the gap that matters most. Good becomes dangerous when it protects a weaker standard from scrutiny and lets people mistake acceptable performance for sustained, compounding strength.
breakdown.deepRead:
The radiology director places the wait-time benchmark beside a handwritten list of delayed cancer follow-ups. One page says the department is meeting the published target. The other says surgeons are losing options because a few suspicious scans return too late. Neither page is false.

The move is to make the good result argue with a better standard. The Collins comparative study has weight because the leap is held against companies close enough to make comfort look costly: 11 good-to-great companies, matched comparisons, and sustained results over a long enough horizon that a lucky spike cannot explain the pattern. The lesson for a smaller room is the same. Do not ask whether the number is respectable. Ask what it is respectable against, what it hides, and whether it keeps improving after the first easy gains are gone.

Comfort hates a fair comparison.

A bookstore owner can feel steady revenue and still lose the browsing traffic that used to create loyal customers. A stadium manager can celebrate high survey scores while the abandoned-line tally grows during the third inning. Good metrics often record the people who stayed, the forms that fit the system, and the outcomes already easy to count. Greatness starts by putting the missing evidence on the same table.

Use the idea with limits. Good is not failure, and contempt for solid work is just another lazy pose. The discipline is narrower: when a good result lowers curiosity, restore curiosity before the standard hardens into a ceiling.
breakdown.fullRead:
A county library director sees the e-card launch hit its signup target. The ribbon photo is ready, the staff message is drafted, and the rural branch pins on the map look small enough to ignore. Then the zip-code heat map lands over the target sheet. Whole towns vanish from the celebrated number.

That is how adequacy does its best hiding. It does not arrive as decay. It arrives as a number that can be defended, a comparison group that flatters, a deadline met with no question about who was left outside the result. Good is the enemy of great because good can end the investigation too early. It gives the room a respectable reason to protect the old standard.

What would you compare the good result with if you were not trying to protect it?

Daniel's scanner report shows the same pressure in a clinical setting. A green benchmark can be true and still leave three urgent names circling on a follow-up list. The work is not to distrust every green light. It is to ask which human consequence the green light cannot see.

The useful comparison is rarely dramatic. Put official success beside the consequence it may be erasing. Put revenue beside foot traffic, departures beside missed connections, survey averages beside the people who left the line. Then stretch the time horizon. Sustained results are harder to fake than a good month, a clean launch, or one loud win. Cumulative momentum shows up when the same standard keeps producing strength after the novelty fades.

The famous research frame matters here because it refuses the easy story. The good-to-great leap is not treated as a mood or a speech. It is held against matched comparisons, which means the question is not whether success happened, but whether a different discipline explains why one similar company kept building while another stayed merely acceptable. That pressure keeps the idea from becoming a poster about wanting more.

A river outfitter with no reportable injuries can still be running a fragile season if wet incident cards pile up around one rock-garden rapid. An airport gate can depart inside the accepted window while a family with a stroller tag watches its connection close. The official number may be useful. It is not sovereign.

The counter-objection is fair: if every good result is challenged, people can feel punished for progress. That is not the move. The point is to separate celebration from certification. Celebrate the honest gain, then ask the question that protects it from becoming complacency. Good work deserves a harder standard, not because it is worthless, but because it may be strong enough to carry one.

Good is not the enemy because it is bad. Good is the enemy because it can sound final. When the green light on the console makes everyone exhale, look once more at the list under the binder clip. The next leap often begins with the evidence a respectable result made easy to ignore.

examples.title: Daniel circles the scan list

planSpec.audience: a radiology director whose department meets the published wait-time benchmark
planSpec.stakes: patients with suspicious scans are still waiting long enough for surgeons to lose treatment options
planSpec.requiredBeat: the director places the benchmark report beside a handwritten list of delayed cancer follow-ups and circles the gap between acceptable and great care

examples.scenario: Daniel opens Monday's review packet under the green scanner-console glow while MRI request forms lean against the keyboard. The benchmark report says the department meets the regional wait-time target. Beside it, a resident has left a handwritten list of delayed cancer follow-ups. Daniel circles three names where surgeons lost treatment options and must decide whether to praise the benchmark or reopen the standard.
examples.whatToDo: Place the two pages in the same review and ask what great care would require for suspicious scans, even if the published benchmark is technically met.
examples.whyItMatters: A benchmark can certify acceptable flow while hiding the cases where delay does real damage. The comparison must expose the gap that comfort would miss.

examples.title: Claire reads the door counter

planSpec.audience: a store owner proud of steady monthly revenue
planSpec.stakes: steady sales hide the loss of browsing traffic that used to create loyal customers
planSpec.requiredBeat: the owner pins last year's receipt roll beside this year's door-counter tape and sees that the same dollars now come from fewer, less curious buyers

examples.scenario: It took Claire until the receipt roll curled over the checkout drawer to see what steady revenue had hidden. Last year, the front table pulled browsers past staff picks all Saturday. This year, she pins the receipt roll beside the door-counter tape and sees the same dollars coming from fewer, hurried buyers. The front display gap near the poetry shelf suddenly looks less like tidiness and more like lost loyalty.
examples.whatToDo: Keep revenue on the page, but add browsing traffic and repeat discovery as the harder standard for the front table.
examples.whyItMatters: Good sales can come from a shrinking base. The missing traffic shows whether the store is building loyal demand or merely harvesting the shoppers who still arrive.

examples.title: Lukas counts the abandoned line

planSpec.audience: an operations manager whose food stands score well on postgame surveys
planSpec.stakes: fans abandon long lines during the third inning and never show up in satisfaction averages
planSpec.requiredBeat: the manager stands behind the pretzel warmer and marks every fan who leaves the line before ordering, then compares that count with the cheerful survey score

examples.scenario: Steam fogs the pretzel warmer while the home team comes to bat and Lukas stands behind the register with a pencil stub. The postgame surveys praise the food stands, but the third-inning horn sounds as nine fans leave the line before ordering. Lukas marks each exit on an abandoned-line tally and has to decide whether the cheerful survey score is measuring the people who stayed rather than the demand that walked away.
examples.whatToDo: Pair the survey score with the abandoned-line tally, then redesign the stand around lost orders during pressure innings.
examples.whyItMatters: Satisfied customers are only part of the evidence. The people who leave before buying never reach the survey, so good averages can hide broken flow.

examples.title: Aanya overlays the heat map

planSpec.audience: a library director whose e-card launch met its signup target
planSpec.stakes: rural patrons remain absent even though the rollout is being celebrated as successful
planSpec.requiredBeat: the director lays a zip-code heat map over the signup target sheet and sees the empty towns the target allowed everyone to ignore

examples.scenario: You unlock the reference desk before opening and find Aanya smoothing a laminated county map under a coffee mug. The e-card launch hit its signup target, so the board packet calls it a success. Then she lays the zip-code heat map over the target sheet and sees three rural branch pins sitting in blank space. Her postmortem is not about effort. It is about the empty towns the target let everyone ignore.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the signup target as one measure, but add rural coverage by zip code and assign outreach to the towns that disappeared from the average.
examples.whyItMatters: A target can be met by the easiest audience. The heat map forces the good number to answer for who was excluded from the gain.

examples.title: Camille sorts the wet cards

planSpec.audience: an outfitter owner proud of a season with no reportable injuries
planSpec.stakes: near misses on one rapid show that no-injury status is hiding a fragile operation
planSpec.requiredBeat: the owner asks guides to sort wet incident cards by rapid and watches one rock garden form a pile that the official injury log never showed

examples.scenario: Camille hears a guide ask, "No injuries means the season was clean, right?" as damp incident cards dry on the paddleboard rack. She predicts the official injury log will match the crew's memory. Then she has the guides sort the wet cards by rapid, and the rock-garden rapid forms its own swollen pile. She must decide whether no reportable injuries is a safety result or a warning label written in quieter ink.
examples.whatToDo: Treat near misses as part of the standard. Rework guide briefing and boat spacing for the rock-garden rapid before the clean injury log becomes an excuse.
examples.whyItMatters: No injuries can hide repeated exposure to the same weak point. Near-miss evidence shows whether the operation is actually safer or merely lucky.

examples.title: Marta replays the amber scanner

planSpec.audience: a gate supervisor whose flights depart within the airline's accepted window
planSpec.stakes: families with tight connections still miss flights while the station reports on-time success
planSpec.requiredBeat: the supervisor replays the scanner timestamps for one family and watches the acceptable departure metric erase their missed connection

examples.scenario: Marta asks which number matters more, the departure window or the family watching the next gate close. She replays the scanner timestamps after the evening bank clears. The boarding scanner had blinked amber beside a stroller tag, and the flight still departed inside the accepted window. On the replay, one family loses its connection by four minutes while the station report keeps its on-time success.
examples.whatToDo: Add connection-window misses to the departure review and make the station explain both numbers before calling the shift reliable.
examples.whyItMatters: On-time departure can be a good operating result and still erase the passenger outcome that reveals whether reliability is strong enough.

questions.prompt: A city clinic reports that 91 percent of appointments start within the official window, but the diabetes nurse shows you a list of patients who wait so long they leave before education visits. Which response best applies the good-to-great move?
choices: Put the official window beside the abandoned education visits and ask what standard would protect the harder outcome
Celebrate the 91 percent because official measures are the only fair measures
Discard all timing data because one list of missed visits proves the metric is useless
questions.explanation: The first choice makes the good metric argue with the ignored consequence. Celebrating the official window hides the gap, while throwing away all data loses a useful but incomplete signal.

questions.prompt: A museum shop has steady revenue after moving expensive gifts to the front, but membership signups from casual visitors have fallen for six months. What is the stronger next question?
choices: Which premium product should get a larger display next month?
What comparison shows whether revenue is replacing the visitor path that used to create members?
How can staff explain the revenue success more confidently to trustees?
questions.explanation: The membership decline is the missing evidence behind the good revenue. More display space or better messaging keeps attention on the flattering number instead of the weakening engine.

questions.prompt: A software team calls a launch great because press coverage tripled. Two weeks later, daily active use is below the old beta level. Which interpretation fits best?
choices: The launch was great because outside attention is the cleanest measure of momentum
The launch failed completely, so no lesson from the press coverage matters
The press spike may be good news, but sustained use is the harder test of whether strength is building
questions.explanation: The correct answer separates a bright event from cumulative momentum. Treating press as proof is too easy, and calling it total failure ignores that good signals can still be useful.

questions.prompt: A school district beats the provincial average in reading, but its closest comparison districts are improving twice as fast and families are transferring out. What should leaders avoid?
choices: Using the provincial average as a shield against the matched comparison and transfer data
Asking whether the comparison districts reveal a stronger standard
Studying transfer patterns alongside reading gains before setting next year's target
questions.explanation: The shield is the problem: a broad average can make comfort look rational. The other choices put the good result under a tougher comparison instead of treating it as final.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team has had no lost-time injuries for a year, yet near-miss cards cluster around one loading bay during rain. Which move shows disciplined use of good results?
choices: Remove the near-miss cards so the team stays proud of the injury record
Keep the injury record visible and treat the wet-bay cluster as the next standard to beat
Announce that the safety program is broken because the near misses exist
questions.explanation: This keeps the honest win without letting it close the investigation. Hiding near misses protects comfort, while declaring total failure punishes progress instead of improving it.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit raises a record amount at one gala after a surprise corporate check, while recurring donors decline. What evidence would best distinguish a spike from momentum?
choices: The number of photos shared from the gala
The largest single donation of the night
The change in repeat gifts and donor retention after the event
questions.explanation: Repeat gifts and retention show whether the engine changed after the spike. Photos and the largest check may explain excitement, but they do not prove sustained results.

questions.prompt: An operations lead says, "Our customer score is above target, so we should stop digging into complaints from the people who left before service." What is the best reply?
choices: The score matters, but the people who left are exactly the comparison that tells us whether good is hiding a ceiling
Complaints from people who left are always more reliable than satisfied-customer scores
Above-target scores mean the system is already great unless revenue falls
questions.explanation: The reply uses both signals and asks what the score omits. The tempting extremes either replace one incomplete measure with another or let a good target end the inquiry.

questions.prompt: A founder wants to call a quarter great because sales were stable during a hard market. You can ask one question before the board vote. Which one is most useful?
choices: Can we make the slide design feel more confident?
Will investors punish us if we describe the quarter as merely good?
Stable against whom, over what horizon, and with what sign that the engine is getting stronger?
questions.explanation: The question forces comparison, duration, and evidence of strength. Slide polish and investor fear both steer the room toward appearance rather than the quality of the result.

questions.prompt: A team leader worries that challenging a good result will sound ungrateful to people who worked hard. Which framing keeps the discipline without punishing progress?
choices: Celebrate the honest gain, then ask what harder evidence would show that the gain can last
Skip the celebration so people understand that good work is never enough
Avoid the harder question until morale is perfect
questions.explanation: The first choice separates appreciation from certification. Skipping celebration turns rigor into contempt, while waiting for perfect morale lets the good result harden into a ceiling.

reviewCards.front: A metric meets target, but a handwritten list shows people still harmed. What question should you retrieve?
reviewCards.back: Ask what stronger comparison the good metric must face. The goal is not to discard the metric, but to expose the consequence it may be hiding.

reviewCards.front: A one-night spike makes the room call the work great. What evidence tests whether it is momentum?
reviewCards.back: Look for sustained behavior: repeat use, retention, referrals, or compounding results over time. A spike can be useful without proving the engine has changed.

reviewCards.front: A broad average flatters your team while close peers are improving faster. What is the move?
reviewCards.back: Use the closer comparison. Good can hide inside a weak reference group, so matched peers often reveal whether comfort is protecting a lower ceiling.

reviewCards.front: People fear that questioning good work will demoralize the team. What distinction matters?
reviewCards.back: Separate celebration from certification. Honor the gain, then test whether it can last and whether it hides a gap that good teams should want to see.

reviewCards.front: A respectable result makes everyone less curious. What is the warning sign?
reviewCards.back: Good has become a ceiling when it ends investigation. Restore curiosity by putting the official result beside ignored consequences, harder comparisons, and time.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is turning a good result into a comparison instead of a conclusion. You keep the honest gain visible, then put it beside the ignored consequence, closer peer, or longer time horizon that reveals whether strength is really compounding.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a dashboard tile is green, then write the one harmed user, missed case, or excluded group the tile might be hiding before you call the result strong.
If a result looks good against a broad average, then compare it with the closest serious peer before setting next year's standard.
If praise makes a project feel successful, then check repeat behavior before adding a victory story to it.
If a no-problem record looks clean, then inspect near misses and abandoned attempts before assuming the system is safe or reliable.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within 24 hours, choose one good result and place it beside one ignored consequence from the same work. Write the harder comparison in a single sentence.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, review three good metrics and label each as proof, partial signal, or comfort shield. Pick one comfort shield and add the missing evidence to the next review.

memorableLines.why: It turns the research logic into a short retrieval cue.

memorableLines.text: Good is not the enemy because it is bad. Good is the enemy because it can sound final.
memorableLines.why: It captures the central paradox without slipping into generic ambition.

memorableLines.text: Good work deserves a harder standard, not because it is worthless, but because it may be strong enough to carry one.
memorableLines.why: It keeps rigor from sounding like contempt for solid work.
